page.title: HeyPace — a screen-aware assistant for Mac
page.description: Ask Pace about your screen, launch apps, and control your browser from the Mac menu bar. Explore interactive diagrams and custom Powers in the development build.

hero.title: ask about *the screen in front of you.*
hero.lede: Ask Pace to explain an unfamiliar control, point to it, or take the next step for you. Work from the menu bar with a local planner or connect Codex with your permission.
hero.note: Public preview 0.3.20 · macOS 26+ · Apple Silicon. Start by typing a question.

window.title: Pace · Command Center
window.alt: Pace Command Center showing a taught automation and the built-in local action list

hero.caption: Pace’s Command Center shows a saved routine alongside the actions it can run.

blocks.title: from a question *to an action.*
blocks.lede: Open Pace over the app you’re using. Start with a question you can check against the screen, then give it a task.

points.title: Understand a screen
points.body: Turn on Read My Screen and ask “What does this message mean?” Pace can explain the current view and point to a target.

points.title: Work across apps
points.body: Open an app or a Chrome profile, scroll a document, or ask for sourced research. Desktop and browser actions use Peekaboo and Playwright.

points.title: Return to a routine
points.body: Teach Pace a sequence you repeat, or ask it to open Codex in Warp in the project folder you choose.

blocks.title: what would you like *Pace to do?*
blocks.lede: In the development build, hold Right Option to speak or type into the notch. Spoken questions get a voice reply. Typed conversations stay quiet.

points.title: Teach with a diagram
points.body: Ask “Show me how an airplane works.” Rotate the model, select a part, and play a narrated walkthrough. Closing the diagram stops its narration.

points.title: Add a Power
points.body: Describe a greeting that plays a GIF and says thank you. Save it as a Power, run it by name, and change it later. Powers can also display drawings and interactive cards.

points.title: Pick up where you left off
points.body: Create and complete tasks in Apple Reminders, resume a coding session, or opt into Watch mode for a suggestion you can ask Pace to explain.

blocks.title: choose what *leaves your Mac.*
blocks.lede: Local planning can use models on your Mac. If you choose Codex, the prompt and any permitted screen context go to that provider. The amber indicator marks off-device planning, and Pace records the request in its local audit log.

blocks.title: without uploading *the meeting.*
blocks.lede: Pace records your mic and the other side’s audio as separate tracks. Transcription runs on your Mac. A privacy-pinned local model writes the summary, action items, and decisions, even when you use a cloud planner elsewhere. Recordings and notes follow your retention window — 30 days by default.

blocks.title: a bigger brain *only when you say so.*
blocks.lede: The planner runs on your Mac by default. Settings → Planner lets you choose a consented Codex or Claude CLI, or a bring-your-own-key API. An off-device turn tints the capsule amber and writes to the local audit log. External integrations are your choice, off by default.

blocks.title: keep control *as Pace works.*
blocks.lede: Enable actions when you want Pace to operate an app. It can request approval before acting, report a missed target, and offer undo for supported changes. Meeting notes and conversation history are stored on your Mac.

blocks.title: voice *and* screen *and* actions.
blocks.lede: Pace starts with voice, current-screen context, and visible computer actions. Read the source-linked field comparison to see where the other Mac assistants fit and where Pace is behind.

blocks.title: try it free. *$29 once* for the local stack.
blocks.lede: The free preview uses Apple Foundation Models on macOS 26. The one-time purchase covers the current release and bundled local models. Payment, delivery, support, included updates, and any refund terms are confirmed before payment through the manual email path.
blocks.note: Apple Silicon only. Review the current release notes and installation steps on the download page.

items.a: Download 0.3.20 for Apple Silicon on macOS 26 or later. Type a question about your screen to start. Voice and hotkey accuracy were outside that release’s hardware checks. Right Option, interactive figures, and Add a Power are in the 0.3.21 development build.

In the development build, a Power gives Pace a capability you can call by name. A workflow saves a sequence of actions. With Add a Power you can describe a new greeting or teaching card, save it, then run or edit it without rebuilding Pace.

items.q: What can Pace send to Codex?
items.a: With cloud planning enabled, Pace sends the request and relevant context to the provider you selected. Screen questions can include a screenshot when Read My Screen is enabled. Provider accounts, limits, and charges apply.
You can ask about the screen for a single turn. In the development build you can also enable Watch mode for background observations and suggestions. Choosing a suggestion starts an explanation.

items.q: Where do my meeting notes go?
items.a: Pace stores recordings and notes under ~/Library/Application Support/Pace/meetings/. Transcription and meeting-note synthesis run on the Mac, including when you use Codex for other tasks.
No. The public preview supports Apple Foundation Models on compatible Macs. LM Studio is an optional way to run larger models locally.
The public preview is free. The optional local model bundle is $29 once. The pricing page explains purchase terms and delivery. External AI providers bill separately under their own terms.
